---
title: "Ordinal regression"
---

The earlier pages introduced [categorical responses](../random-variables-and-distributions/bernoulli-and-categorical-distributions.qmd) and the [logit link](link-functions.qmd). Ordinal regression uses those ideas when the response categories have a known order but no defensible numerical spacing. A commitment response of *no*, *maybe*, or *yes* places *maybe* between the two endpoints. It does not establish that the change from *no* to *maybe* is the same size as the change from *maybe* to *yes*.

Coding the categories as 1, 2, and 3 and fitting a linear regression adds that equal spacing assumption. Deleting *maybe* and fitting a binary logistic regression changes the response and discards the observations that may reveal uncertainty. [**Ordinal regression**](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat504/lesson/8/8.1) keeps the order while leaving the distance between adjacent categories unspecified.

This page introduces the cumulative logit model. It reuses the earlier probability, logit, linear-predictor, and categorical-response concepts.

## Replace category scores with cumulative events

Let the ordered response be

$$
Y_i\in\{\text{no},\text{maybe},\text{yes}\}.
$$

The order creates two cumulative events:

$$
Y_i\leq\text{no}
$$

and

$$
Y_i\leq\text{maybe}.
$$

The first event contains only *no*. The second contains *no* and *maybe*. The remaining probability belongs to *yes*.

An ordinal model thus does not assign a numerical distance to the category labels. It models the probability of falling at or below each boundary in the ordered response.

## Introduce two ordered cutpoints

Let

$$
\eta_i=\mathbf{x}_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta
$$

be the linear predictor. Introduce cutpoints $\kappa_1<\kappa_2$. The cumulative logit model is

$$
\operatorname{logit}\Pr(Y_i\leq c)
=\kappa_c-\eta_i,
\qquad c\in\{1,2\}.
$$

The cutpoints divide an ordered latent location into the three recorded response regions. The ordering constraint matters. If $\kappa_1$ exceeded $\kappa_2$, the probability of being at or below *no* could exceed the probability of being at or below *maybe*.

Using the logistic cumulative distribution function $F(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})$, the category probabilities are

$$
\Pr(Y_i=\text{no})=F(\kappa_1-\eta_i),
$$

$$
\Pr(Y_i=\text{maybe})
=F(\kappa_2-\eta_i)-F(\kappa_1-\eta_i),
$$

and

$$
\Pr(Y_i=\text{yes})=1-F(\kappa_2-\eta_i).
$$

These probabilities are nonnegative and sum to one. Increasing $\eta_i$ moves probability toward higher categories.

## Calculate one condition by hand

Suppose

$$
\kappa_1=-.8,
\qquad
\kappa_2=1,
\qquad
\eta_i=0.
$$

The probability of *no* is

$$
F(-.8)\approx.310.
$$

The cumulative probability through *maybe* is

$$
F(1)\approx.731.
$$

Thus the probability of *maybe* is

$$
.731-.310=.421,
$$

and the probability of *yes* is

$$
1-.731=.269.
$$

Now suppose a predictor raises the linear predictor from zero to one. The new probabilities are

$$
\Pr(Y_i=\text{no})=F(-1.8)\approx.142,
$$

$$
\Pr(Y_i=\text{maybe})=F(0)-F(-1.8)\approx.358,
$$

and

$$
\Pr(Y_i=\text{yes})=1-F(0)=.500.
$$

The one unit location shift reduces *no* probability, slightly reduces *maybe* probability, and raises *yes* probability. An ordinal coefficient is not a constant change in any one category probability. The complete response scale interpretation requires all three predicted probabilities.

## Interpret one coefficient at both boundaries

Suppose $x_i$ increases by one and its coefficient is $\beta$. Because the model uses $\kappa_c-\eta_i$, a positive coefficient reduces the cumulative log odds at every cutpoint. Equivalently, it multiplies the odds of falling above each cutpoint by $e^\beta$.

For the three category response, the same coefficient describes both of these comparisons:

1. *maybe* or *yes* compared with *no*;
2. *yes* compared with *no* or *maybe*.

This shared coefficient is the [**proportional odds assumption**](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat504/lesson/8/8.1). The model assumes that a predictor shifts the response upward through one common location change rather than having a separate effect at each boundary.

The assumption does not say that the category probabilities change by the same amount. They generally do not, as the hand calculation shows. It says that one log odds coefficient applies to both cumulative partitions.

## Fit the model in R

The response must be an ordered factor whose level order matches the linguistic scale:

```r
judgments$commitment <- ordered(
  judgments$commitment,
  levels = c("no", "maybe", "yes")
)

fit_commitment <- ordinal::clm(
  commitment ~ embedding_environment,
  data = judgments,
  link = "logit"
)
```

The formula specifies the location predictor. The model estimates two cutpoints because the response has three categories. Reversing the factor levels reverses the direction of the fitted location scale, so the level order must be inspected before any coefficient is interpreted.

Predicted category probabilities provide the most direct summary:

```r
new_environments <- data.frame(
  embedding_environment = levels(judgments$embedding_environment)
)

predict(
  fit_commitment,
  newdata = new_environments,
  type = "prob"
)
```

The output should be reported as a row of probabilities for each environment. A statement that one condition has a coefficient of 1.2 on an unnamed latent scale leaves the linguistic response implicit.

## Check the shared shift

A predictor may primarily distinguish *no* from the other responses while doing little to separate *maybe* from *yes*. In that case, a single shared coefficient can conceal a category specific pattern. The proportional odds assumption should thus be checked against predicted and observed category distributions at theoretically relevant predictor values.

Sparse categories create another limitation. If *no* responses are rare, the first boundary has little information. A model may estimate a broad upward shift while the data provide weak evidence about how that shift is divided between the two cumulative comparisons.

The present model also treats rows as conditionally independent. Repeated judgments from the same participant or repeated discourses require a dependence model introduced after the mixed effects foundation.

::: {.callout-note title="Check the order"}
If a predictor has a positive coefficient, which response direction receives more probability? Why does this sign depend on the order of the factor levels? What common restriction connects the two cumulative comparisons?
:::

## What ordinal regression adds

Ordinal regression models ordered categories through cumulative events and ordered cutpoints. It preserves the category order without assuming equal numerical spacing. One location coefficient shifts every cumulative logit under the proportional odds assumption, so interpretation should return to the full set of category probabilities. After the mixed effects foundation, [ordinal mixed models](ordinal-mixed-models.qmd) add repeated participant and item structure to this response model.
